title: Approximate Control and Deep Q-Networks
oneLiner: Learning which action to take when situations are described by features or raw pixels, and the two tricks (replay and target networks) that make Q-learning with neural networks work.

what.html:
To choose actions in huge state spaces, we estimate action values with a formula or network: q̂(state, action). Training uses the same SARSA or Q-learning targets as before, but adjusts shared weights. A Deep Q-Network (DQN) is Q-learning with a neural network that reads the screen, plus experience replay (learn from a shuffled memory of past moments) and a target network (a frozen copy used to compute targets).

Everyday versionRevising from a shuffled pile of past exam questions (replay) beats only re-reading today's notes; and checking your answers against last week's answer key (frozen target) is calmer than against an answer key you rewrite after every question.

why.html:
• DQN learned to play many Atari games from pixels with one set of settings.
  • Each trick fixes a specific failure of naive Q-learning with neural networks.
  • It's the template for most value-based deep RL.

how.title: Score actions with features
how.html: Describe each state–action pair with features (e.g. "obstacle close", "jumping") and score it as a weighted sum. In the dino game: no-op now 1.0, no-op next 1.5, jump next 2.5.

how.title: SARSA with features
how.html: Target = reward + γ × value of the action you actually take next: 2 + 0.2 × 1.5 = 2.30. Only the weights of active features move: θ₁ goes from 1.0 to 2.17.

how.title: Q-learning with features
how.html: Target = reward + γ × best next value: 2 + 0.2 × 2.5 = 2.50, giving θ₁ = 2.35. More aggressive, and riskier with approximation.

how.title: Taming optimism
how.html: If both next actions are really worth 2.0, the honest target is 2.40. Q-learning's max gives 2.50 (too high). Double Q picks the action with one network and scores it with another: 2.28.

how.title: Replay memory
how.html: Consecutive game frames are nearly identical, which confuses a network. Store recent experiences and train on random handfuls from across the memory; each experience also gets reused many times.

how.title: Freeze the target
how.html: Compute targets with a copy of the network that's only updated every few thousand steps, so the network isn't chasing a target that moves every time it learns. Double DQN: the live network chooses, the frozen copy scores.

demo.html: A toy picture of why the frozen target matters: when updates leak into their own target (as with shared network weights), the online estimate runs away; with a frozen target it moves only one controlled step per sync. Try different sync periods.

example.html:
Same transition, three targets. Dino game, reward 2, γ = 0.2, current value 1.0. SARSA (next action no-op, worth 1.5): 2.30. Q-learning (best next, 2.5): 2.50. Double Q (choose jump with θ, score it with θ′ = 1.4): 2.28. With α = 0.9 the active weight becomes 2.17, 2.35 or 2.152.

Supplementary In our tiny DQN experiment, a network without replay and a target network still found the goal but its value estimates exploded to about 200,000 instead of −12.5.

misunderstandings: DQN is a new learning rule.
It's Q-learning's target with a network and stabilisers.
Replayed data come from old policies, so learning is off-policy.
A good greedy policy means good values.
Values can diverge while the action ranking still works.
It needs a max over discrete actions.
takeaways: q̂(s, a, θ) = θᵀφ(s, a); update only active features.
Worked targets: SARSA 2.30, Q-learning 2.50, Double Q 2.28.
Experience replay: decorrelate and reuse data.
Target network θ⁻: stable targets; Double DQN decouples select/evaluate.
thirty: Approximate control represents action values as q̂(s, a, θ) = θᵀφ(s, a) (or a network with one output per action) and updates θ ← θ + α[U − q̂]∇q̂. In the dino example (θ = [1, 0.5, 1], γ = 0.2, α = 0.9, r = 2), SARSA's target is 2.30 (θ₁ → 2.17), Q-learning's 2.50 (θ₁ → 2.35), above the honest 2.40 because of maximisation bias, and Double Q's 2.28 (θ₁ → 2.152). Q-learning with approximation embodies the deadly triad. DQN stabilises it with experience replay (random mini-batches from a buffer of past transitions: decorrelation and reuse) and a target network θ⁻ synced every C steps; Double DQN selects with the online network and evaluates with the target network.
